title: Scales and Modes
goal: Play the major scale and its relative minor as movable shapes, run sequences through them, and hear Dorian and Mixolydian as one changed note over a band.
assumes: You can fret and pick single notes and play eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM. Knowing the pentatonic box helps and isn't needed. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; a scale is learned when your ear knows it, which takes many short visits.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM

orderRationale: The major scale first as a sound and a formula on one string, then as one movable shape, because every other scale here is described as a change to it. A key is named as soon as the shape has been moved, because moving it is changing key. The relative minor comes next: the same notes from a different home, which is the idea a mode rests on. Keys are met again in A and F before the relative minor, and the relative minor again in E minor and D minor before the Level ends. The seven chords of a key open the Intermediate Level, because they need only the shapes already known, and they come just before harmonic minor, because its raised note is first heard as a change to one of those chords. Harmonic minor is one raised note, and it prepares the ear for the modes, which are also one changed note each. Sequences then turn a shape into something the fingers know in any order. The second major shape waits until C major has been carried across two positions, because it is the lower of those two given a name. Dorian comes before Mixolydian because it sits on the minor shape players already have. Each mode is then played from a second string and over new chords before the player is asked to choose between them. Once both modes are known, the pentatonic notes are shown with two added to make each one, and the same seven notes are played from three homes after the second key. The Level ends by choosing a second time, with the changing note written out before the player chooses alone.
gradingLimits: The app checks that the notes you played were the written ones, after the take, and times them. It can tell a wrong note from a right one, which is what matters in a scale. It cannot tell whether you heard the changed note as a colour or just played the fret, and it cannot judge the 'your turn' Exercises at all. Naming notes and scale degrees out loud is taught and not heard. None of this has been tried on a real guitar yet.

steps.title: The major scale
steps.goal: Play a major scale in open position and along one string, and know the pattern of whole and half steps that makes it.
steps.why: The major scale is the ruler everything else is measured with. Chords and every other scale in this Path are named by comparing them to it. It is seven notes in a fixed pattern of steps: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. On one string you can see that pattern laid out in frets.
howTo: A whole step is two frets and a half step is one. From any note, the pattern two, two, one, two, two, two, one gives its major scale.
Say the numbers 1 to 8 as you go up. The eighth note is the first one again, an octave higher.
In C major's open position each fret has its own finger: first finger for fret 1, second for fret 2, third for fret 3. For G the hand sits one fret higher.
steps.payoff: A tune everybody knows, played from the scale you just learned.

steps.title: One shape for every key
steps.goal: Play the major scale as one closed shape with no open strings, two octaves, and move it to other keys.
steps.why: Open position gives you two or three keys. A shape with no open strings gives you all twelve: move the hand and the key changes. This shape starts with the second finger on the root on the low E string, and it is the one most players learn first.
howTo: For A major the second finger is on the low E string at fret 5. The hand covers frets 4 to 7, one finger per fret, and never moves.
The root is under the second finger on the low E string, the fourth finger on the D string, and the second finger on the top string.

To change key, move the whole hand so the second finger is on the new root. The note names on the low E string tell you which key that is: fret 5 is A, fret 8 is C, fret 10 is D, and Know the Neck teaches the rest.
steps.payoff: One fingering that plays a major scale in any key, and a melody that follows three chords with it.

steps.title: What a key is
steps.goal: Play the major shape in C, G and D by name, say which notes each key sharpens, and find the first, fourth and fifth notes of a key under a band.
steps.why: When you moved the shape, you changed key. A key is the seven notes of one major scale together with the note they call home, the root of the scale, and it takes its name from that home. C major is the key with no sharps and no flats. Every other key needs some, because the pattern of whole and half steps stays the same wherever it starts: G major has one sharp, F#, and D major has two, F# and C#. The first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale are the ones a band leans on: the three main chords of a key are built on them.
howTo: The shape is the same in every key. With the second finger on the low E string at fret 8 the scale is C major. Two frets higher, at fret 10, it is D major.

The low four strings are tuned the same distance apart, so the same fingers work from the A string. With the second finger on the A string at fret 10 the scale is G major. G major is also at the low E string's fret 3; it is played from the A string here so that it sits under the same hand as D.

Count the scale as you play it, 1 to 8. The fourth note is under the second finger too: the same fret as the root, on the next higher string. The fifth note is two frets above the fourth, under the fourth finger.
A sharp is not a special kind of note. It is where the pattern of steps lands when the scale starts on G or on D.
The Exercise with the band comes round in four keys: C, G, D and A. A major is the same shape with the second finger on the low E string at fret 5, and it has three sharps: F#, C# and G#.
steps.payoff: Three keys you can name, the three notes a band's chords stand on, and one tune played in two keys.

steps.title: Two more keys: A and F
steps.goal: Play A major and F major by name, say which notes each key sharpens or flattens, and find the first, fourth and fifth notes of both under a band.
steps.why: C, G and D are three keys you have named, and A you have met under the band. Two more by name turn the examples into something you can work out for yourself. A major carries on the way G and D went: it keeps their sharps, F# and C#, and adds G#. Each of those keys starts on the fifth note of the one before. F major goes the other way: C is its fifth note. It is the first key with a flat. Its fourth note is one fret above A, and it is called B flat, not A sharp, for one reason: a scale uses every letter once. F, G, A, then a B of some kind, C, D, E. Calling it A sharp would use A twice and leave B out.
howTo: A major is the shape with the second finger on the low E string at fret 5. Its three sharps are C# on the A string's fret 4, and F# and G# on the D string's frets 4 and 6.
Going C, G, D, A, each key keeps the sharps of the one before and adds one. The new sharp is always the seventh note of the new key, one fret below its root: F# under G, C# under D, G# under A.
A flat lowers a note one fret, as a sharp raises it one. B flat is one fret below B: the D string's fret 8, where C major has B at fret 9. A chord chart writes it Bb.
F major is played from the A string here, second finger on fret 8, so that it sits under the same hand as C major from the low E string's fret 8.
steps.payoff: Five keys you can name, C, G, D, A and F, and a tune in the first flat key.

Land each bar's first note with the band.
Wait for the band's '1' before each bar.
Hold each long note its two beats, then move.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Land on the root as the last chord comes.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

variants.label: F major
variants.purpose: The first, fifth and fourth notes of the scale, in that order, as single notes over a band, through the chords built on them. This Take is in F major, from the A string.
howTo: Quarter notes and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
In F, bar 1 counts up from home: F, G, A, B flat, the A string's frets 8 and 10, then the D string's frets 7 and 8. They are notes one, two, three and four.
Bar 2 is note five, C, the D string's fret 10: the chord changes to C as you reach it. Bar 3 steps back down to note four, B flat, the D string's fret 8. Bar 4 is F again.
The chords are F, C, B flat and F. Each time the chord changes, the note you are on is the note that chord is named after.

Count up the scale from the root to each note.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.

Land each bar's first note with the band.
Wait for the band's '1' before each bar.

Keep the pick close as you cross strings.

All of it sits at fret 7 on the A, D and G strings. Bar 2 starts on B flat, the D string's fret 8, and climbs to a long F, the G string's fret 10.
Bar 3 starts on E, the G string's fret 9, and bar 4 ends on a long F, the A string's fret 8.
B flat is in bars 1, 2 and 4, always the D string's fret 8 under the second finger.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

cues.say: Start each bar on a note of its chord.
Keep B flat on the D string's fret eight.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play just the notes on the tab, no more.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Wait for the band's '1' before each bar.
Hold the long F two beats, then come in.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
End on the long F and let it ring two beats.

steps.title: The relative minor
steps.goal: Play the natural minor scale as a shape, and hear that it is a major scale started from its sixth note.
steps.why: Every major scale has a minor scale hiding in it: the same seven notes, with the sixth note as home. C major from A is A minor. Nothing about the notes changes; what changes is which one sounds like the end of the sentence. That idea, same notes and a new home, is all a mode is.
howTo: The minor shape starts with the first finger on the root on the low E string. For A minor that is fret 5: frets 5, 7 and 8 on the low two strings, 5 and 7 on the D string.
Play C major, then the same notes from A. Listen for how the mood changes when A becomes home.

Compared with a major scale from the same root, the third, sixth and seventh notes are each one fret lower. Hear it once in your own time: A major in the movable shape, then A minor, both from the low E string's fret 5.
steps.payoff: The same seven notes played twice, once bright and once dark, and a minor melody over a band.

exercises.title: The minor shape, one octave

In A: low E string 5, 7 and 8; A string 5, 7 and 8; D string 5 and 7. Fingers 1, 3 and 4 on the low two strings, 1 and 3 on the D string.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Fingers one, three, four on the low two strings.
Play the third three frets above the root.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play two notes to each click, no more.
Put each beat's first note on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the held note out, then start again.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Come down as evenly as you went up.

variants.label: B minor

howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
In B: low E string 7, 9 and 10; A string 7, 9 and 10; D string 7 and 9.

variants.label: C minor
variants.purpose: C natural minor on the low three strings, up and back. A different key comes round on each Take.

exercises.title: The same notes, two homes
exercises.purpose: C major up and back from the A string's fret 3, then A minor up and back from the low E string's fret 5. Seven notes, played twice, and they do not sound alike.

exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. Which half sounded finished to you, and on which note?

cues.say: Listen for home: C first, then A.
Start C on the A string, A on the low E string.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play two notes to each click, no more.
Put each beat's first note on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the long note's beat, then go on.
Move the hand during each long note.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Come down to the low A and hold it a beat.

exercises.title: A melody over Am, Dm and Em
exercises.purpose: A four-bar tune in A minor over a band, starting each bar on a note of its chord: A, then D, then E, and E again on the way home to A.
howTo: Quarters and eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
All of it sits in the minor shape at fret 5 on the low three strings.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

cues.say: Start each bar on a note of its chord.
Keep it all in the minor shape at fret five.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play just the notes on the tab, no more.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Wait for the band's '1' before each bar.
Hold the long A two beats, then come in.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
End on the low A and let it ring two beats.

steps.title: The relative minor in other keys
steps.goal: Find the relative minor of G major and of F major on the neck, play E minor and D minor from the A string, and play a tune in E minor over a band.
steps.why: A minor came out of C major: the same seven notes with the sixth note as home. Every major key has a relative minor found the same way. G major from its sixth note is E minor, and it keeps G major's one sharp, F#. F major from its sixth note is D minor, and it keeps F major's one flat, B flat. On the neck there is a shortcut that works in every key: the minor root is three frets below the major root on the same string. (On the next lower string it is two frets above, on the low four strings, which is where you found A minor before.)
howTo: From the major root, step down the string two scale notes: one fret, then two. From G at the A string's fret 10 that is F# at fret 9 and E at fret 7. You know both ends of this already: C major starts on the low E string's fret 8 and A minor on fret 5, three frets below it.
The minor shape works from the A string as it does from the low E string, first finger on the root. For E minor that is frets 7, 9 and 10 on the A and D strings and frets 7 and 9 on the G string.
It goes the other way too: from a minor root, the major key with the same notes is three frets up the string.
steps.payoff: Two more minor keys, E minor and D minor, each found from the major key it shares its notes with, and a minor tune over a band.

exercises.title: From G down to E minor
exercises.purpose: The root of G major, two scale notes down the string to its sixth note, E, and then the same seven notes with E as home: E minor, said by name.
howTo: Quarter notes, one to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80; bar 1 ends on a half note.
Bar 1 is on the A string: G at fret 10, F# at fret 9, then a long E at fret 7. Fingers 4, 3 and 1: the hand is already where E minor is played.
Bars 2 and 3 climb E minor: A string 7, 9 and 10, D string 7, 9 and 10, G string 7 and 9. Say E, F#, G, A, B, C, D, E.
Bar 4 comes back down as far as A, the D string's fret 7. When the line goes round, bar 1 finishes the descent: G, F#, E.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and steady quarters after the take. The names are yours to say.

cues.say: Say each name from E to E as you climb.
Play F sharp at the A string's fret nine.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play one note on each click, no more.
Have the next finger ready before the click.
Wait for the click before each new note.
Hold the long E two beats, then climb.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Keep coming down: A, then G, F sharp, E.

selfCheck: Did you say each note's name, or its number in the scale, as you played it?

exercises.title: G major, then E minor: one sharp
exercises.purpose: G major up and back from the A string's fret 10, then E minor up and back from fret 7 on the same string. The same seven notes, with F# in both, and they do not sound alike.
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 2 are G major with the first finger at fret 9: A string 10 and 12, D string 9, 10 and 12, G string 9, 11 and 12, and back down.
Bars 3 and 4 are E minor with the first finger at fret 7: A string 7, 9 and 10, D string 7, 9 and 10, G string 7 and 9, and back down.
Hold the long G, then move the hand down two frets as it ends. After the long E the hand goes back up for the repeat.
The F# is the G string's fret 11 in G major and the A string's fret 9 in E minor.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. Which half sounded finished to you, and on which note?

cues.say: Listen for home: G first, then E.
Keep F sharp in both halves of the line.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play two notes to each click, no more.
Put each beat's first note on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the long note's beat, then go on.
Move two frets as each long note ends.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Come down to the long E, then back up for G.

exercises.title: D minor, then F major: one flat
exercises.purpose: The other way round: D minor up and back from the A string's fret 5, then F major up and back from fret 8, three frets higher on the same string. Both have B flat and no other flat or sharp.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 2 are D minor with the first finger at fret 5: A string 5, 7 and 8, D string 5, 7 and 8, G string 5 and 7, and back down.
Bars 3 and 4 are F major with the first finger at fret 7: A string 8 and 10, D string 7, 8 and 10, G string 7, 9 and 10, and back down.
Hold the long D, then move the hand up two frets as it ends. After the long F the hand goes back down for the repeat.
The B flat is the D string's fret 8 in both halves: under the fourth finger in D minor and under the second in F major.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Listen for home: D first, then F.
Keep B flat on the D string's fret eight.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play two notes to each click, no more.
Put each beat's first note on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the long note's beat, then go on.
Move two frets as each long note ends.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
Come down to the long F, then back to D.

exercises.title: A melody over Em, Am and Bm
exercises.purpose: A four-bar tune in E minor over a band, starting each bar on a note of its chord: B, then A, then D, and G on the way home to E.
howTo: Quarters, eighths and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
All of it sits in the minor shape at fret 7 on the A, D and G strings. Bar 2 climbs to a long E, the G string's fret 9, and bar 4 ends on a long E an octave lower, the A string's fret 7.
The F# is the A string's fret 9, in bars 3 and 4.
The chords stand on notes one, four and five of E minor: E, A and B.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

cues.say: Start each bar on a note of its chord.
Play F sharp at the A string's fret nine.
Press right behind each fret so it rings.
Play just the notes on the tab, no more.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Wait for the band's '1' before each bar.
Hold the long E two beats, then come in.
Keep the pick close as you cross strings.
End on the lower E and let it ring two beats.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.difficultyException: The relative minor again in two more keys, at the pace of the Step before. Its first Exercise is slow on purpose: quarter notes, to find the minor root on one string and say the names.

steps.title: Chords from the scale
steps.goal: Build the seven chords of a key by taking every other note of its scale, play them as single notes in C major and from A, and play two lines over a band that follow them.
steps.why: A chord is not a separate thing to learn beside a scale. Start on any note of the scale, skip one, play the next, skip one, play the next: those three notes are a chord. Do it from each of the seven notes and you have the seven chords of the key. In C major they are C, D minor, E minor, F, G, A minor and B diminished. Playing the movable shape in thirds, in the Beginner Level, was the first two notes of each chord without the names. It is why a band's chords and your scale agree, and why a note of the chord sounds at home while that chord is playing. A three-note chord like these is called a triad. This Step is a first look: Triads puts them under the hand, and Chords in a Key puts the seven of them into songs.
howTo: The three notes have names. The one the chord starts from is its root, the next is its third and the last is its fifth: they are the first, third and fifth notes counting up the scale from the root.

Some of the chords come out major and some minor, because the steps of the scale are not all the same size. Counted along one string, a major chord's third is four frets above its root and a minor chord's is three. In every major key the order is the same: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
The chord on the seventh note is the odd one: its third and its fifth are each one fret lower than a major chord's, and it is called diminished. Play it, hear that it does not rest, and move on.
Say each chord's name on its long note. The small m you have seen in the charts means minor: Dm is D minor.
steps.payoff: The seven chords of a key under one hand, the same seven counted from A, and two lines over a band made from the notes of its chords.

exercises.title: The seven chords of a key
exercises.purpose: C major's seven chords as single notes, one after another up the scale: root, third and fifth from each note. A different key comes round on each Take.
howTo: Two eighths and a quarter note for each chord, two chords to a bar, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
The notes: C, E, G; D, F, A; E, G, B; F, A, C; G, B, D; A, C, E; B, D, F; then C, E, G again an octave higher. Each group starts one scale note above the last.
Every note is in the C major shape with the first finger at fret 7, one finger to a fret. The line starts on the low E string's fret 8 and ends on the B string's fret 8.

After most long notes the same finger plays the next root: same fret, one string lower. Hop it across, or roll the fingertip over, and let the long note be a little short. When the line goes round, the second finger drops from the B string to the low E string at the same fret.
Say the names on the long notes: C, D minor, E minor, F, G, A minor, B diminished, C.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and time after the take. The names are yours to say.

variants.label: D major
variants.purpose: D major's seven chords as single notes, one after another up the scale: root, third and fifth from each note. The fingers are the same in every key, and so is the order of major and minor.
howTo: Two eighths and a quarter note for each chord, two chords to a bar, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
The notes: D, F#, A; E, G, B; F#, A, C#; G, B, D; A, C#, E; B, D, F#; C#, E, G; then D, F#, A again an octave higher. Each group starts one scale note above the last.
Every note is in the D major shape with the first finger at fret 9, one finger to a fret. The line starts on the low E string's fret 10 and ends on the B string's fret 10.

After most long notes the same finger plays the next root: same fret, one string lower. Hop it across, or roll the fingertip over, and let the long note be a little short. When the line goes round, the second finger drops from the B string to the low E string at the same fret.
Say the names on the long notes: D, E minor, F# minor, G, A, B minor, C# diminished, D.

variants.label: A major
variants.purpose: A major's seven chords as single notes, one after another up the scale: root, third and fifth from each note. The fingers are the same in every key, and so is the order of major and minor.
howTo: Two eighths and a quarter note for each chord, two chords to a bar, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
The notes: A, C#, E; B, D, F#; C#, E, G#; D, F#, A; E, G#, B; F#, A, C#; G#, B, D; then A, C#, E again an octave higher. Each group starts one scale note above the last.
Every note is in the A major shape with the first finger at fret 4, one finger to a fret. The line starts on the low E string's fret 5 and ends on the B string's fret 5.

After most long notes the same finger plays the next root: same fret, one string lower. Hop it across, or roll the fingertip over, and let the long note be a little short. When the line goes round, the second finger drops from the B string to the low E string at the same fret.
Say the names on the long notes: A, B minor, C# minor, D, E, F# minor, G# diminished, A.

exercises.title: The same seven chords from A
exercises.purpose: A minor has the notes of C major, so it has the same seven chords. Counted from A they come in a new order: A minor, B diminished, C, D minor, E minor, F, G.
howTo: Two eighths and a quarter note for each chord, two chords to a bar, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80; the last note is a half note.
The notes: A, C, E; B, D, F; C, E, G; D, F, A; E, G, B; F, A, C; G, B, D; then a long A.

The first finger is at fret 2 and each finger keeps its own fret. The line starts with the fourth finger on the low E string's fret 5 and ends with the first finger on the G string's fret 2. Most new roots are under the finger that just played the long note, same fret, one string lower.
The fifth chord, E minor, is E, G and B: the D string's frets 2 and 5, then the G string's fret 4. The next Step raises that G to G#, which makes the chord E major.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and time after the take. The names are yours to say.

exercises.title: Chord notes, then a walk to the next root
exercises.purpose: Four bars over C, F, G and C with a band. Each of the first three bars plays its chord's root, third and fifth, then walks down the scale into the root of the next chord.
howTo: Three quarter notes and two eighths in each of the first three bars, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90; bar 4 ends on a half note.
Bar 1: C, E, G, then A, G and into F. Bar 2: F, A, C, then B, A and into G. Bar 3: G, B, D, then E, D and into C.
Bar 4 is the C chord from that higher C: the D string's fret 10, the G string's fret 9 and a long G on the B string's fret 8.
It starts on the low E string's fret 8, in the shape at fret 7. On beats 1, 2 and 3 you are playing the chord of the bar, one note at a time.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A tune that lands on chord notes
exercises.purpose: A four-bar tune over C, A minor, F and G with a band. It is a tune, not a run of chord notes, and it still starts every bar on a note of that bar's chord.
howTo: Quarters, eighths and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bar 1 starts on E, the third of C. Bar 2 starts on A, the root of A minor, and ends on a long C, its third.
Bar 3 starts on F, the root of F, and ends on A, its third. Bar 4 starts on B, the third of G, and ends on a long D, its fifth.
It sits in the shape at fret 7 on the D, G and B strings, and starts with the third finger on the G string's fret 9.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Harmonic minor
steps.goal: Play A harmonic minor, and use its raised seventh to pull back to A over an E7 chord.
steps.why: Natural minor has a weak ending: G to A is a whole step, and it drifts home. Raise the G to G# and the pull is strong, because G# is the third of E7, the chord that leads back to A minor. E7 is an E major chord with one more scale note, D, on top. One note changed, and the scale goes from folk song to something darker. It is also practice for the modes: one note, a new colour.
howTo: Take the minor shape and raise the seventh note one fret: on the D string, fret 5 becomes fret 6.
The gap from F to G# is three frets, on two strings: the A string's fret 8 to the D string's fret 6.
Play G# over E7 and A over Am. The first asks a question and the second answers it.
steps.payoff: A phrase over Am and E7 where one note makes the chord change audible.

exercises.title: The shape with a raised seventh
exercises.purpose: A harmonic minor, one octave up and back: the minor shape with G# at the D string's fret 6.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 5, 7, 8; A string 5, 7, 8; D string 6 and 7. The second finger takes fret 6 and the third takes fret 7.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. The raised seventh is the note to listen for.

variants.label: B harmonicMinor
variants.purpose: B harmonic minor, one octave up and back: the minor shape with A# at the D string's fret 8.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 7, 9, 10; A string 7, 9, 10; D string 8 and 9. The second finger takes fret 8 and the third takes fret 9.

variants.label: C harmonicMinor
variants.purpose: C harmonic minor, one octave up and back: the minor shape with B at the D string's fret 9.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 8, 10, 11; A string 8, 10, 11; D string 9 and 10. The second finger takes fret 9 and the third takes fret 10.

variants.label: D harmonicMinor
variants.purpose: D harmonic minor, one octave up and back: the minor shape with C# at the D string's fret 11.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 10, 12, 13; A string 10, 12, 13; D string 11 and 12. The second finger takes fret 11 and the third takes fret 12.

exercises.title: G# over E7, A over Am
exercises.purpose: Four bars over Am and E7. The Am bars use the plain minor notes and come to rest; the E7 bars lean on G# and want to move.
howTo: Eighths and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bars 1 and 3 are over Am. Bar 2 starts on G#, the D string's fret 6; bar 4 starts on E and ends on G#. All of it stays in the shape at fret 5.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

exercises.title: Natural, then harmonic
exercises.purpose: The minor shape up and back with G, then up and back with G#. One fret apart, and the second one sounds like a different country.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 2: D string 5 and 7. Bars 3 and 4: D string 6 and 7. Everything else is the same.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

steps.difficultyException: Slower than the Step before it on purpose: there is one new note to hear, and a chord change to hear it against.

steps.title: Harmonic minor in a second key
steps.goal: Play E harmonic minor from the A string, use its D# over B7, and play a line over the three main chords of a minor key that raises the seventh only over the fifth chord.
steps.why: The raised seventh is not a fact about A minor. In any minor key the chord on the fifth note comes out minor when you build it from the scale, and raising the scale's seventh note one fret turns that chord major and gives it a pull back home. In E minor the seventh note is D and the fifth chord is built on B: raise D to D# and the B chord turns from minor to major, because D# is its third. That is why the chord is B7 here where the tune in E minor had B minor. The 7 in B7 is one more scale note, A, stacked on top of the chord. The note that matters here is the D#. The raised note belongs to that one chord. Over the other chords of the key, the plain minor scale is still the one that fits.
howTo: Take the E minor shape from the A string, first finger at fret 7, and raise the seventh note one fret: on the G string, fret 7 becomes fret 8.
The raised seventh is always one fret below the root. D# at the G string's fret 8 sits under E at fret 9.
Play D# over B7 and E over Em. Over Em and Am, when you want the seventh note, play D.
steps.payoff: E minor with both of its sevenths, and eight bars over Em, Am and B7 where one note follows the chord.

exercises.title: The raised seventh from the A string
exercises.purpose: E harmonic minor, one octave up and back: the minor shape from the A string with D# at the G string's fret 8. E minor on one Take, D minor on the next.
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
A string 7, 9 and 10; D string 7, 9 and 10; G string 8 and 9. The second finger takes fret 8 and the third takes fret 9.
From C on the D string's fret 10 to D# on the G string's fret 8 is three frets' distance, counted along one string: the widest step in the scale.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. The raised seventh is the note to listen for.

variants.label: D harmonic minor
variants.purpose: D harmonic minor, one octave up and back: the minor shape from the A string with C# at the G string's fret 6. It is the same shape as E harmonic minor, two frets lower.
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
A string 5, 7 and 8; D string 5, 7 and 8; G string 6 and 7. The second finger takes fret 6 and the third takes fret 7.
From B flat on the D string's fret 8 to C# on the G string's fret 6 is three frets' distance, counted along one string: the widest step in the scale.

exercises.title: E minor: natural, then harmonic
exercises.purpose: The E minor shape up and back with D, then up and back with D#. One fret apart, and only the second one pulls toward E.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 2: G string 7 and 9. Bars 3 and 4: G string 8 and 9. Everything else is the same: A string 7, 9 and 10, D string 7, 9 and 10.
The first finger plays the D at fret 7 and the second finger plays the D# at fret 8.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

exercises.title: D# over B7, E over Em
exercises.purpose: Four bars over Em and B7 with a band. The Em bars come to rest; the B7 bars end on D# and want to move.

Bars 1 and 3 are over Em, and each ends on a long G, the A string's fret 10. Bars 2 and 4 are over B7, and each ends on a long D#, the G string's fret 8.
Bar 3 starts on E, the G string's fret 9: one fret above the D# that bar 2 was holding. All of it stays in the shape at fret 7.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

The chords are Em, Am, Em, B7, then Em, Am, B7, Em. The D, the G string's fret 7, is in bars 2, 3 and 5. The D#, fret 8, is in bars 4 and 7.
Bar 4 climbs to a long D#. Bar 5 answers with E, then D on the way down, with only the E between the two sevenths.
All of it stays in the shape at fret 7 on the A, D and G strings, and it ends on a long E, the A string's fret 7.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

steps.title: Sequences
steps.goal: Run a scale in threes, in fours and in thirds, up and down, without losing the pattern.
steps.why: Up and down is how you learn where the notes are. Sequences are how you learn to get from any one of them to any other. Three notes up, start one higher, three more: the fingers have to know every neighbour of every note, and that is what makes a scale usable in a solo.
howTo: In threes, each group starts one scale note higher than the last. Say the first note of each group.
Triplets for threes, so each group fills one beat. Eighths for fours, so each group fills two. Rhythm Foundations teaches triplets in its Intermediate Level, in the Step 'Three to a beat'.
Count '1-trip-let, 2-trip-let'. Three even notes a click, with the first one on it.
When the pattern breaks down, stop and find the last group you were sure of. Start again from there.
steps.payoff: A minor in threes, fours and thirds: the three patterns most scale-based licks are cut from.

exercises.title: In threes
exercises.purpose: A, B, C; B, C, D; C, D, E: A minor climbing in groups of three, one group to a beat.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 75.
The minor shape at fret 5, one octave. The first note of each group lands on the click, and each group starts where the last one's second note was.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even triplets after the take.

variants.label: B minor
variants.purpose: B, C#, D; C#, D, E; D, E, F#: B minor climbing in groups of three, one group to a beat.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 75.
The minor shape at fret 7, one octave. The first note of each group lands on the click, and each group starts where the last one's second note was.

variants.purpose: C, D, Eb; D, Eb, F; Eb, F, G: C minor climbing in groups of three, one group to a beat.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 75.
The minor shape at fret 8, one octave. The first note of each group lands on the click, and each group starts where the last one's second note was.

variants.label: D minor
variants.purpose: D, E, F; E, F, G; F, G, A: D minor climbing in groups of three, one group to a beat.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 75.
The minor shape at fret 10, one octave. The first note of each group lands on the click, and each group starts where the last one's second note was.

exercises.title: In fours
exercises.purpose: A, B, C, D; B, C, D, E; and on up: groups of four in eighth notes, each group two beats long.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
The first note of each group is on beat 1 or beat 3. Lean on it a little so you can hear where each group starts.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

variants.label: B minor
variants.purpose: B, C#, D, E; C#, D, E, F#; and on up: groups of four in eighth notes, each group two beats long.

variants.label: C minor

variants.label: D minor

exercises.title: In thirds
exercises.purpose: A to C, B to D, C to E, up the octave: every other note of the scale, which is how chords are built.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
Each pair skips one scale note. Some pairs sit on one string and some cross to the next; the shape under your hand decides.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

variants.label: B minor
variants.purpose: B to D, C# to E, D to F#, up the octave: every other note of the scale, which is how chords are built.

variants.label: C minor
variants.purpose: C to Eb, D to F, Eb to G, up the octave: every other note of the scale, which is how chords are built.

variants.label: D minor
variants.purpose: D to F, E to G, F to A, up the octave: every other note of the scale, which is how chords are built.

exercises.title: In threes, coming down
exercises.purpose: The descending pattern from C on the G string: C, B, A; B, A, G; and on down to the low A. Going down is its own skill.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, 50 BPM up to a pass at 75.
The first finger reaches back to fret 4 on the G string for the B. Each group starts one scale note lower than the last.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even triplets after the take.

steps.difficultyException: Its passes sit lower than the band lines that end the Step before, because triplets are new here. The demand is the pattern: every group starts one scale note on, in both directions.

steps.title: Two positions, and three notes per string
steps.goal: Carry C major from one position into the next, and play it three notes per string at the eighth fret.
steps.why: One shape is a box. A scale covers the whole neck, and there are two common ways to get out of the box: shift from one position into the one above it, or use three notes on every string, which climbs the neck by itself. Both are the same seven notes you already know.
howTo: The shift happens on the G string: finish the lower shape on fret 5 with the fourth finger, then play the same fret again with the first finger and carry on up.
Three notes per string at the eighth fret: frets 8, 10 and 12 on the low two strings, 9, 10 and 12 on the next two.
Keep the thumb behind the neck so the hand can open for the wider shape. Nothing here should hurt.
steps.payoff: C major across two positions without a seam, and a three-notes-per-string run that covers four strings in one bar.

exercises.title: C major, two positions
exercises.purpose: Up through the shape at the second fret, across into the shape at the fifth, to the top string and back the same way.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
The G string's fret 5 is played twice in a row: once with the fourth finger to end the lower shape, once with the first to start the upper one. That repeat is the shift.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. The shift is where the time moves.

exercises.title: Three notes per string
exercises.purpose: C major from the low E string's fret 8 across four strings, three notes on each, up in one bar and down in the next. Alternate Picking and Legato work on this fingering in their Steps 'Three notes per string'.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
One string to a beat. Fingers 1, 2 and 4 on the low two strings (8, 10, 12) and 1, 2 and 4 again on the next two (9, 10, 12), with the hand a fret higher.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even triplets after the take.

exercises.title: The formula, then the shape
exercises.purpose: A major scale along one string and then the same scale in the movable shape: the same eight notes found two ways.
howTo: Quarter notes along the string, then eighths in the shape, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
On the G string from fret 2: 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13, 14 and back. It is A major. Then the same scale in the shape at fret 4, from the low E string's fret 5.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and steady quarters after the take.

steps.difficultyException: The lines move at the same eighth-note rate as the sequences before them but repeat no note, so the metric reads lower. The demand is the shift and the wider three-per-string hand.

steps.title: A second shape, and the two joined
steps.goal: Play the major scale from a root on the A string, join that shape to the one from the low E string, and play a tune that uses both.
steps.why: The Step before this carried C major out of one position into the next. The lower of those positions was the low half of this shape: a major scale with its root on the A string, under the second finger. It gets a name of its own here because, together with the shape from the low E string, it gives every key two places on the neck, five frets apart. Join them and a key is no longer one box.
howTo: In D the second finger is on the A string at fret 5 and the first finger covers fret 4. On the A, D and G strings the fingers are the ones the first shape uses on its low three strings: 2 and 4, then 1, 2 and 4, then 1, 3 and 4.
The B string is tuned one fret lower than the pattern of the other strings, so on the top two strings every note sits a fret higher. Move the hand up one fret to meet them: first finger on fret 5.

The first shape for the same key is five frets higher: in D, second finger on the low E string at fret 10. To join the two, shift on the G string: fourth finger on fret 7, then first finger on fret 9.
steps.payoff: D major from fret 4 to fret 12 in one line, and a tune that answers itself an octave higher.

exercises.title: The shape from the A string
exercises.purpose: The whole second shape: from the root on the A string up to the top string, back down past the root to the low E string, and round again. A different key comes round on each Take.
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
In D: A string 5 and 7, D string 4, 5 and 7, G string 4, 6 and 7. Then the hand moves up one fret: B string 5, 7 and 8 with fingers 1, 3 and 4, top string 5 and 7 with fingers 1 and 3.

On the way down the hand moves back as you return to the G string. Below the root there are three more notes: A string 4, then low E string 7 and 5. The line turns there and climbs back to the A string's fret 4, one note under the root, ready to go round again.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. The move between the G and B strings is where the time slips.

variants.label: C major
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
In C: A string 3 and 5, D string 2, 3 and 5, G string 2, 4 and 5. Then the hand moves up one fret: B string 3, 5 and 6 with fingers 1, 3 and 4, top string 3 and 5 with fingers 1 and 3.

On the way down the hand moves back as you return to the G string. Below the root there are three more notes: A string 2, then low E string 5 and 3. The line turns there and climbs back to the A string's fret 2, one note under the root, ready to go round again.

variants.label: E major
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
In E: A string 7 and 9, D string 6, 7 and 9, G string 6, 8 and 9. Then the hand moves up one fret: B string 7, 9 and 10 with fingers 1, 3 and 4, top string 7 and 9 with fingers 1 and 3.

On the way down the hand moves back as you return to the G string. Below the root there are three more notes: A string 6, then low E string 9 and 7. The line turns there and climbs back to the A string's fret 6, one note under the root, ready to go round again.

exercises.title: One octave, two places
exercises.purpose: The same eight notes twice: from the A string in the second shape, then from the low E string in the first shape, five frets higher. A different key comes round on each Take.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
In D, bars 1 and 2 go up and back from the A string's fret 5, with the first finger at fret 4. Bars 3 and 4 go up and back from the low E string's fret 10, with the first finger at fret 9.

The fingers are the same in both halves, and so are the notes: the low E string's fret 10 is the same D as the A string's fret 5. Hold the last note of each half, then move the hand as it ends: up five frets for bars 3 and 4, and back down for the repeat.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

variants.label: C major
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
In C, bars 1 and 2 go up and back from the A string's fret 3, with the first finger at fret 2. Bars 3 and 4 go up and back from the low E string's fret 8, with the first finger at fret 7.

The fingers are the same in both halves, and so are the notes: the low E string's fret 8 is the same C as the A string's fret 3. Hold the last note of each half, then move the hand as it ends: up five frets for bars 3 and 4, and back down for the repeat.

variants.label: E major
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
In E, bars 1 and 2 go up and back from the A string's fret 7, with the first finger at fret 6. Bars 3 and 4 go up and back from the low E string's fret 12, with the first finger at fret 11.

The fingers are the same in both halves, and so are the notes: the low E string's fret 12 is the same E as the A string's fret 7. Hold the last note of each half, then move the hand as it ends: up five frets for bars 3 and 4, and back down for the repeat.

exercises.title: The two shapes joined
exercises.purpose: Two octaves in one line: up through the second shape, across into the first on the G string, to the root on the top string and back the same way. A different key comes round on each Take.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

In D, bar 1 is the second shape from the A string's fret 5 up to the G string's fret 7. Bar 2 starts with the shift: first finger to the G string's fret 9, then 11 and 12, B string 10 and 12, top string 9 and 10.
On the way down the shift is in bar 3: after the G string's fret 9 with the first finger, the fourth finger takes fret 7.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. The shift is where the time moves.

variants.label: C major
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

In C, bar 1 is the second shape from the A string's fret 3 up to the G string's fret 5. Bar 2 starts with the shift: first finger to the G string's fret 7, then 9 and 10, B string 8 and 10, top string 7 and 8.
On the way down the shift is in bar 3: after the G string's fret 7 with the first finger, the fourth finger takes fret 5.

variants.label: E major
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

In E, bar 1 is the second shape from the A string's fret 7 up to the G string's fret 9. Bar 2 starts with the shift: first finger to the G string's fret 11, then 13 and 14, B string 12 and 14, top string 11 and 12.
On the way down the shift is in bar 3: after the G string's fret 11 with the first finger, the fourth finger takes fret 9.

exercises.title: A tune across both shapes
exercises.purpose: Eight bars in D over a band. The tune is played low in the second shape, then again an octave higher in the first shape, and each bar starts on a note of its chord.
howTo: Quarters, eighths and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bars 1 to 4 sit at fret 4, on the low four strings. Bar 4 dips below the root to the low E string's frets 7 and 5, and ends on a long D, the A string's fret 5.

Hold that long D, then move the hand up to fret 9 as it ends. Bars 5 to 8 are the same tune an octave higher, starting with the fourth finger on the D string's fret 12 and reaching the top string's fret 10 in bar 6. After the last note the hand goes back down to fret 4 for the repeat.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Dorian
steps.goal: Play A Dorian, hear its raised sixth against natural minor, and use it over Am and D.
steps.why: Dorian and Mixolydian are modes. In the Beginner Level a mode was the same notes from a new home. Here you meet each one the other way, as a scale you know with one note changed, and the Step 'One scale, three homes' joins the two. Dorian is the minor scale of rock, funk and a lot of blues: natural minor with the sixth note raised a half step. In A that is F# where the minor scale has F. It sounds brighter, and it is the right scale whenever a minor chord is followed by the major chord a fourth above it, as in Am to D, because F# is the third of D.
howTo: In the minor shape, the sixth note is the A string's fret 8. Dorian moves it up to fret 9, or, easier, to the D string's fret 4 under the first finger.
Play the minor version and then the Dorian version of the same phrase. Only one note moves.
Over the D chord, land on F#. That is the note that proves the scale.
steps.payoff: A phrase over Am and D that could not have been played with the minor scale.

exercises.title: The Dorian shape
exercises.purpose: A Dorian, one octave up and back: A, B, C, D, E, F#, G, A, with F# at the D string's fret 4.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 5, 7, 8; A string 5 and 7; D string 4, 5 and 7. The first finger reaches back one fret for the F#.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. F# is the note to listen for.

variants.label: B dorian
variants.purpose: B Dorian, one octave up and back: B, C#, D, E, F#, G#, A, B, with G# at the D string's fret 6.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 7, 9, 10; A string 7 and 9; D string 6, 7 and 9. The first finger reaches back one fret for the G#.

variants.label: C dorian
variants.purpose: C Dorian, one octave up and back: C, D, Eb, F, G, A, Bb, C, with A at the D string's fret 7.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 8, 10, 11; A string 8 and 10; D string 7, 8 and 10. The first finger reaches back one fret for the A.

variants.label: D dorian
variants.purpose: D Dorian, one octave up and back: D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D, with B at the D string's fret 9.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Low E string 10, 12, 13; A string 10 and 12; D string 9, 10 and 12.

exercises.title: Minor, then Dorian
exercises.purpose: Two phrases, each played with F and then with F#. The first of each pair is natural minor and the second is Dorian.
howTo: Eighths and half notes, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 3 use the A string's fret 8, F. Bars 2 and 4 use the D string's fret 4, F#, in its place.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and time after the take. The difference between the bars is one note; hear it before you move on.

exercises.title: A Dorian phrase over Am and D
exercises.purpose: Four bars over a band going from Am to D and back. The bars over D start on F#, the note that belongs to both the chord and the scale.
howTo: Eighths, quarters and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bars 1 and 3 start on A; bars 2 and 4 start on F#, the D string's fret 4. The whole phrase stays between frets 4 and 8.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.difficultyException: A new scale starts here with one shape and a side-by-side comparison, at an easier pace than the eight bars over three chords that end the Step before. The demand is hearing the one changed note.

steps.title: Mixolydian
steps.goal: Play A Mixolydian, hear its lowered seventh against the major scale, and use it over A and G.
steps.why: Mixolydian is the major scale of rock and blues: a major scale with the seventh note lowered a half step. In A that is G where the major scale has G#. It is the scale that fits a seventh chord such as A7. It also fits every song that goes from a major chord to the major chord a whole step below it, as in A to G.
howTo: From A on the low E string's fret 5: A, B, C#, D, E, F#, G, A. The C# is on the A string's fret 4, under the first finger.
Play the phrase with G# (the D string's fret 6), then with G (fret 5). The first is plain major; the second is Mixolydian.
Over the G chord, land on G. Over the A chord, C# tells everyone it is major.
steps.payoff: A phrase over A and G with the sound of a hundred classic rock songs in it.

exercises.title: The Mixolydian shape
exercises.purpose: A Mixolydian, one octave up and back: major, with G natural at the D string's fret 5.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
Low E string 5 and 7; A string 4, 5 and 7; D string 4, 5 and 7. First finger on the frets at 4, second on 5, fourth on 7.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take. G natural is the note to listen for.

variants.label: B mixolydian
variants.purpose: B Mixolydian, one octave up and back: major, with A natural at the D string's fret 7.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
Low E string 7 and 9; A string 6, 7 and 9; D string 6, 7 and 9. First finger on the frets at 6, second on 7, fourth on 9.

variants.label: D mixolydian
variants.purpose: D Mixolydian, one octave up and back: major, with C natural at the D string's fret 10.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
Low E string 10 and 12; A string 9, 10 and 12; D string 9, 10 and 12. First finger on the frets at 9, second on 10, fourth on 12.

exercises.title: Major, then Mixolydian
exercises.purpose: Two phrases, each played with G# and then with G. The first of each pair is A major and the second is A Mixolydian.
howTo: Eighths and half notes, 50 BPM up to a pass at 85.
Bars 1 and 3 use the D string's fret 6, G#. Bars 2 and 4 use fret 5, G, in its place.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and time after the take. One fret, and the phrase goes from hymn to rock.

exercises.purpose: Four bars over a band going from A to G and back. The bars over G start on G; bar 1, over A, leans on C#.
howTo: Eighths, quarters and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bar 1 starts on A and bar 3 on E. Bars 2 and 4 start on G, the D string's fret 5, and bar 2 ends on the low G at fret 3.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
